title: Enols and enolates
goal: How a carbonyl compound becomes a nucleophile at its α-carbon, and what that nucleophile attacks.

problemSets.title: Tautomerism
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: A proton moves from the α-carbon to oxygen: the enol, made with acid or with base.
problemSets.conceptCard:
An **enol** is a *tautomer* of its ketone: a different molecule, with a hydrogen moved from the α-carbon to oxygen and C=C in place of C=O. Unlike resonance, tautomerism breaks a C–H bond and makes an O–H bond.

The ketone is far more stable (acetone is about 1 part in 10⁸ enol), but interconversion is fast with a catalyst:

- **acid**: protonate the oxygen first, then water removes the α-proton
- **base**: remove the α-proton first (the **enolate**), then protonate the oxygen

An α-C–H is acidic (pKa about 20 for a ketone) because the enolate shares its charge with oxygen.

setItems.whyThisOne: Acid catalysis: oxygen is protonated before the C–H breaks.
Base catalysis: the same change in the opposite order, through the enolate.

problemSets.title: α-Substitution
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: The enol or enolate attacks a halogen at its α-carbon; in base, a methyl ketone goes on to the haloform reaction.
problemSets.conceptCard:
An enol is an alkene with an oxygen lone pair pushing into it: a good nucleophile at the **α-carbon**. It attacks Br₂ as the oxygen lone pair forms C=O⁺–H.

- In **acid**, enol formation is the slow step and the reaction stops after one halogen: each halogen makes the carbonyl oxygen less basic.
- In **base**, each halogen makes the remaining α-hydrogens *more* acidic, so a methyl group is halogenated three times. Hydroxide then adds to the C=O, and **CX₃⁻** leaves: a rare carbon leaving group. This is the *haloform reaction*.

setItems.whyThisOne: The enol as a nucleophile, and why acid stops at one bromine.
Addition–elimination with CBr₃⁻ as the leaving group.

problemSets.title: Enolate alkylation
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: LDA converts a ketone fully into its enolate, which attacks an alkyl halide by SN2.
problemSets.conceptCard:
**LDA** (lithium diisopropylamide) is strong (pKa of its conjugate acid about 36) and too hindered to add to C=O. At −78 °C it turns a ketone completely into its lithium enolate; then the electrophile is added.

The enolate attacks a methyl or primary alkyl halide by **SN2** through its α-carbon, while the oxygen lone pair re-forms C=O.

An unsymmetrical ketone has two enolates:

- the **kinetic** enolate forms faster: the less hindered proton (LDA, −78 °C, no proton source)
- the **thermodynamic** enolate is more stable: the more substituted C=C (equilibrating conditions)

setItems.whyThisOne: Full deprotonation first, then an SN2 on iodomethane.
Two possible enolates: which one LDA makes at −78 °C.

problemSets.title: The aldol reaction
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: An enolate adds to a second carbonyl compound; heating with base then removes water by E1cB.
problemSets.conceptCard:
With a weak base such as hydroxide, only a little enolate forms, and it attacks the carbonyl compound still present: the **aldol** reaction makes a **β-hydroxy carbonyl** compound.

The α-hydrogen of the aldol is still acidic. Its enolate can push out hydroxide by **E1cB**, giving a conjugated enone: an *aldol condensation*.

A **crossed** aldol is clean when one partner has no α-hydrogens and is the better electrophile, such as benzaldehyde with acetone (the *Claisen–Schmidt* condensation).

setItems.whyThisOne: The basic aldol: an enolate adds to a second aldehyde.
A crossed aldol that goes on to the conjugated enone.

problemSets.title: Checkpoint
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Make the enol or enolate, then decide what it attacks.
problemSets.conceptCard: Reactions from every set, shuffled, names hidden until you finish. Three attempts per step.

setItems.whyThisOne: Aldol and E1cB in one sequence.
